s.g: of land to be submerged under water; of a deluge to set in
x: रौशन : वर्षा हो रही है? सुरेन्द्र : मूसलाधार! जल-थल एक हो रहे हैं।
बादल आते, घटाएँ उमड़तीं, ऐसा मालूम होता कि जल-थल एक हो जायेगा, परन्तु वे आशा की नहीं, दुःख की घटाएँ थीं।

ety.text: Literally, “of land and water to become one”; from जल-थल (jal-thal, “land and water”), एक (ek, “one”), होना (honā, “to become”).

s.g: to take advantage of another's misfortune

ety.text: Literally, "to warm one's hand in a burning house". Compare the Kashmiri proverb أکِس دَزان دٲر تہٕ بیٛاکھ وُشناوان اَتھٕ (literally “one's beard is burning and another warms their hand”) with a similar meaning.
Borrowed from Classical Persian جادو (jādū), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *yaHtúš. Doublet of यातु (yātu). Compare Assamese যাদু (zadu), Bengali জাদু (jadu), Marathi जादू (jādū).
Related with झपटना (jhapaṭnā, “to swoop down; to go quickly”) and झपाट (jhapāṭ, “quickness”).
Ultimately from Old Norse Danmǫrk

ety.text: Literally, “of breath to come in nose”; from दम (dam, “breath, life”) + नाक (nāk, “nose”) + में (mẽ, “in”) + आना (ānā, “to come”).

s.g: attractive, interesting, engaging, pleasant, lovely, charming, winsome

ety.text: Borrowed from Classical Persian دِلْکَش (dilkaš, “charming”). By surface analysis, दिल (dil) + कश (kaś).
Alternative form of दिरानी (dirānī) based on देवर (devar). Further, from Prakrit 𑀤𑁂𑀅𑀭𑀸𑀡𑀻 (dearāṇī), from Sanskrit देवरजानी (devarajānī).
Borrowed from Classical Persian پخته (puxta). Compare Punjabi ਪੁਖ਼ਤਾ (puxtā) / پُختہ (puxth), Gujarati પુખ્ત (pukht), Marathi पोक्त (pokta).

s.g: a Peshwa (historical prime minister of the Maratha Empire)

ety.text: Borrowed from Classical Persian پیشوا (pēšvā), from Middle Persian [Book Pahlavi needed] (pyšʾwpʾd /⁠pēšōbāy⁠/, “leader, vanguard”). Compare Punjabi ਪੇਸ਼ਵਾ (peśvā) / پیشوا (peśoā), Gujarati પેશવા (peśvā), Bengali পেশওয়া (peśōẇa), Telugu పీష్వా (pīṣvā), Kannada ಪೇಷ್ವೆ (pēṣve), Tamil பேஷ்வா (pēṣvā), Malayalam പേഷ്വ (pēṣva).

From Prakrit 𑀮𑁄𑀆 (loā), from a denominalization of Sanskrit लोक (loka, “space, world, sight”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“light”) in the sense of "illuminating" and connected to रुच् (ruc, “to shine, illuminate”).
